source.title: Robust Noisy Correspondence Learning via Self-Drop and Dual-Weight
source.authors: Fan Liu; Chenwei Dong; Chuan-Yi Zhang; Hua Zhou; Jun Zhou

page_placements.theme: Mismatched image-text supervision changes alignment and memorization

record.file_problem: Full paper text is present; no apparent truncation or garbling that prevents reading.
record.tranche_reason: The study cites the memorization effect as motivation for a method addressing noisy image-text correspondences. Its results concern that method and correspondence noise, not random-label fitting or the listed claim versions.
record.gate_note: The paper reports image-text retrieval performance under correspondence noise and describes similarity distributions for clean and noisy pairs during training. These do not test the listed random-label claim versions. Results from cited work are not extracted.
record.test_reason: The paper invokes early learning and memorization to motivate noisy-correspondence handling, but evaluates retrieval robustness and mitigation methods. Its own results do not measure random-label training fit, optimization time, or the temporal ordering of learning real and random labels. Figure 5 measures image-text similarity distributions during fine-tuning of pretrained models.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate. The authors conclude that self-drop and dual weighting improve robustness to noisy image-text correspondences, including high noise ratios. They also emphasize that a smaller clean dataset can be more valuable for fine-tuning pretrained vision-language models than a larger noisy dataset.
record.recipe_differences: The study fine-tunes CLIP ViT-B/32 for cross-modal matching using sample dropping and dual weights; it does not apply the original random-label experiments.
record.method_sensitivity: The study varies dataset, correspondence-noise ratio, and training stage; it reports that performance and clean/noisy similarity distributions vary with these conditions.

fits_no_version.finding: On Flickr30K with 40% mismatched correspondences, SDD increasingly separates clean and noisy image-text similarity distributions, whereas NPC's distributions increasingly overlap; NPC's separation at epoch 5 is worse than at epoch 1.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Sample dropping and weighting affect clean/noisy correspondence separation during CLIP fine-tuning.

record.problems: The similarity-distribution result is described qualitatively and shown in a figure; no uncertainty estimate is stated. Results concern correspondence noise rather than random labeling.
record.rows_left_out: No listed claim version is tested. Retrieval comparisons and ablations concern cross-modal correspondence learning and do not directly measure the claimed random-label behaviors.

untested.parts: Near-zero training error on completely random labels, chance test performance, and unchanged architecture and hyperparameters.
Relative training time for true and random labels and convergence speed across corruption fractions.
Training fit on shuffled pixels, independently permuted pixels, and Gaussian-noise inputs.
Perfect training fit alongside steadily increasing test error across random-label corruption fractions.
Whether weight decay, dropout, and augmentation prevent random-label fitting, and whether removing them harms true-label generalization.

Temporal ordering of learning shared real-data patterns and memorizing noisy labels. Pre-existing similarity separation and subsequent correspondence-distribution changes do not establish this ordering.

record.verdict_notes: No verdicts apply to V1–V6. Retrieval degradation with correspondence noise does not establish V4 without training-fit measurements; qualitative noise fitting does not establish V6's learning order.

versions.untested_parts: Random-label fitting, chance test error, and unchanged architecture or training hyperparameters.
Training time for random labels versus true labels and convergence versus corrupted-label fraction.
Classification with randomly corrupted labels, perfect training fit, and test error across corruption fractions.
Effects of weight decay, dropout, or augmentation on random-label fitting and true-label generalization.
Learning real labels before random labels and comparing how real and random labels are learned.

rows.subject: SDD
rows.operation_detail: Visualized similarity distributions for clean and noisy image-text pairs across training stages.
rows.measure: Similarity distribution of clean and noisy pairs; the text reports that clean-pair similarity rises and noisy-pair similarity decreases, with clearer separation.
rows.baseline: Initial epoch: SDD and NPC similarity distributions are the same.
rows.value: After 5 epochs, SDD still performs well in separating clean and noisy samples, although it inevitably fits noise.
rows.note: This is noisy image-text correspondence, not random-label fitting; similarity separation does not establish the listed claim versions.
rows.check: The description matches Section IV-C.3 and Figure 5, but this is the proposed mitigation method's similarity-distribution result. Neither separation of clean and noisy correspondences nor the caption's qualitative statement about fitting noise establishes any listed version.

source_check.locator_found: Figure 5 caption and panels (a)–(d); Section IV-C.3; Section IV-A.2.

rows.subject: NPC
rows.operation_detail: Compared similarity distributions for clean and noisy image-text pairs across training stages.
rows.measure: Similarity distribution of clean and noisy pairs; the text reports increasing overlap during training.
rows.baseline: Initial epoch: SDD and NPC similarity distributions are the same.
rows.value: After 5 epochs, NPC's separation of noise is worse than at epoch 1.
rows.note: The comparison concerns noisy correspondences and does not test random-label fitting.
rows.check: The description matches Section IV-C.3 and Figure 5. Increasing distributional overlap in NPC does not measure random-label fitting or establish that real labels are learned before noise. The clean/noisy distinction already exists at epoch 0 in the pretrained backbone.
